plan: Four passages weighted toward Key Ideas and Details: CLD-P-ACT-R-000078 social science (Dust Bowl, Black Sunday 1935, Hugh Hammond Bennett, 1928 erosion report, Soil Conservation Act 1935, demonstration projects, 1937 model districts law, shelterbelts 1935-42); CLD-P-ACT-R-000079 humanities (Gee's Bend quilts, 1962 ferry closing and 2006 return, 1960s cooperative, 2002 Houston/Whitney exhibition, critique of painting comparisons); CLD-P-ACT-R-000080 natural science/history of technology (longitude problem, 1714 Longitude Act, John Harrison's sea clocks, 1759 timekeeper, 1761-62 Jamaica trial, 1773 payment); CLD-P-ACT-R-000081 original literary narrative (tide-pool walk; patience). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus R074-05 (revision 2) on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000076. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Holding the Soil
passages.text:
On April 14, 1935, a black wall of dust rolled across the southern Great Plains. Witnesses in Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas described the afternoon turning as dark as midnight; drivers stopped their cars because they could not see the road, and families sealed their windows with wet sheets. The storm became known as Black Sunday, and in a news report filed the next day, a reporter used a phrase that would name the whole region and the decade: the "dust bowl."

The storms had natural and human causes. A severe drought had settled over the Plains in the early 1930s, but the land had been made vulnerable long before. For decades, and especially during the wheat boom of the 1910s and 1920s, farmers had plowed up millions of acres of native prairie grass. Those grasses, with roots that reached deep into the ground, had held the soil in place through earlier dry spells. Once the grass was gone and the rain stopped, there was little to keep the topsoil from blowing away.

Few people had warned about this danger as persistently as Hugh Hammond Bennett, a soil scientist with the U.S. Department of Agriculture. As early as 1928, he had co-authored a government report calling soil erosion "a national menace," and he spent years trying to persuade officials that the loss of topsoil was as serious a threat as any flood or crop disease. When Congress finally acted, it moved quickly. The Soil Conservation Act, signed in April 1935, established the Soil Conservation Service, with Bennett as its first chief, and gave the agency broad authority to fight erosion on private as well as public land.

Bennett believed that lectures and pamphlets would not change how people farmed. Instead, the new agency set up demonstration projects, working with volunteer farmers to try new methods on their own fields so that neighbors could see the results for themselves. Farmers were encouraged to plow along the natural contours of the land rather than in straight lines, to plant alternating strips of different crops, to grow cover crops that protected bare soil, and to return the most damaged fields to grass. In 1937, the federal government also proposed a model law that let farmers form local soil conservation districts, which allowed decisions to be made by the people who worked the land.

A separate federal program took a more dramatic approach. Between 1935 and 1942, workers planted more than 200 million trees in long rows called shelterbelts, stretching from the Canadian border to the Texas Panhandle, to slow the wind before it reached open fields.

By the end of the decade, the amount of soil blowing across the Plains had fallen sharply. Historians still debate how much credit belongs to the new farming methods and how much belongs to the rain, which returned in the early 1940s. What is clearer is that the crisis permanently changed how the federal government viewed soil: no longer as an endless resource that each farmer could use however they wished, but as something the nation had a shared interest in protecting.

passages.title: Quilts from the Bend
passages.text:
Gee's Bend, Alabama, sits inside a deep loop of the Alabama River, surrounded by water on three sides. Many of the several hundred people who live there are descendants of people who were enslaved on the cotton plantation that once occupied the land, and many still share the name of the family that owned it. For most of the twentieth century, the community was poor, rural, and difficult to reach.

It was also, for generations, a place where women made quilts. They did so first out of necessity: houses were drafty, and blankets were expensive. The quilters worked with whatever was at hand, including worn-out work clothes, faded denim, feed sacks, and scraps left over from sewing. Because the material varied so much, the quilts did too. Instead of repeating a single block in precise rows, as many traditional patterns do, a Gee's Bend quilt might set large rectangles of color against one another, let a border wander off true, or break a familiar pattern partway across the surface. Quilters learned from their mothers and grandmothers but were expected to work out designs of their own.

The community's isolation deepened in the 1960s. A ferry had long carried residents across the river to the county seat, but in 1962 the service ended, leaving a trip of more than an hour by road. Many residents believed the closing was meant to keep them from reaching the courthouse to register to vote. The ferry did not return until 2006.

Outsiders first took notice of the quilts in the 1960s, when a cooperative founded nearby sold quilts made by local women to department stores in New York. The orders paid well, but buyers often wanted neat, regular patterns, and some quilters set their own improvised designs aside to meet them.

Wider fame came decades later. In 2002, an exhibition called The Quilts of Gee's Bend opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, and then traveled to the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York. Critics were enthusiastic. One wrote that the quilts were among the most remarkable works of modern art the United States had produced, and others compared them to the paintings of famous abstract artists.

Those comparisons helped bring the quilters attention and income, but they can also be misleading. The women of Gee's Bend were not responding to modern painting, which few of them had ever seen. They were working within a tradition of their own, one shaped by scarcity, family teaching, and individual choice. To praise the quilts for resembling museum paintings is, in a way, to suggest that they needed a painter's approval to matter.

passages.title: Keeping Time at Sea
passages.text:
For most of the history of ocean travel, sailors could find their latitude, their position north or south, fairly easily by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon. Longitude, their position east or west, was far harder. Because Earth turns 15 degrees every hour, a navigator who knew both the local time and the time at the ship's home port at the same moment could calculate how far east or west the ship had traveled. Local time could be found from the sun. The problem was keeping track of home-port time across weeks of rolling seas, damp air, and swings in temperature.

The consequences of getting longitude wrong were severe. Ships missed islands where they planned to take on fresh water, sailed into rocks they believed were miles away, or wandered for weeks searching for their destination. In 1714, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act, offering a prize of up to 20,000 pounds, an enormous sum at the time, for a method that could determine longitude at sea to within half a degree.

Many of the leading scientists of the day expected the answer to come from astronomy: from careful observation of the moon's position against the stars, compared with tables calculated in advance. A clock accurate enough to do the job seemed almost impossible. The best clocks on land relied on swinging pendulums, which a ship's motion threw into disorder, and metal parts that expanded and contracted with heat and cold, changing the clock's rate.

John Harrison, a carpenter from the north of England with no formal training in science, decided to attempt it anyway. His early clocks were made largely of wood, and he chose woods that were naturally oily so that the moving parts needed no lubricant, which in other clocks thickened and failed over time. His first sea clock, completed in 1735, was a heavy brass machine that kept good time on a trial voyage. Rather than claim a reward, Harrison asked for support to build a better one.

He spent the next quarter century on the problem. His second and third clocks introduced new solutions to the effects of motion and temperature, but his breakthrough was a fourth timekeeper, finished in 1759, that looked less like a clock than like an oversized pocket watch. On a voyage to Jamaica in 1761 and 1762, it lost only about five seconds over 81 days at sea.

Even so, the Board of Longitude, the panel responsible for awarding the prize, was slow to pay. Its members demanded further trials, required Harrison to explain his design in detail and hand over his clocks, and continued to favor the astronomical method. Only in 1773, after Harrison appealed to King George III, did Parliament grant him a large payment, though never the official prize itself. Harrison died three years later. Within a few decades, however, copies of his design, known as marine chronometers, were becoming standard equipment on ocean-going ships.

passages.title: The Bathtub Pool
passages.text:
Mara had agreed to spend July with her aunt Teresa on the condition that there would be internet, and there was, technically, if she stood at the end of the driveway and held her phone above her head. Teresa ran tide-pool walks for tourists along a stretch of rocky coast, and on the third morning, when Mara ran out of excuses, she went along.

The tourists were a family of five and a retired couple with matching hats. Teresa led them across the slick black rocks to a pool about the size of a bathtub and crouched at its edge. "Now," she said, "we wait."

Mara looked into the water. She saw rocks, a few limp strands of seaweed, and her own impatient face. One of the children asked what they were waiting for. "For the pool to forget we're here," Teresa said.

It took longer than Mara thought anyone would tolerate. Her knees ached. A gull complained overhead. Then a rock she had been staring at for two full minutes moved, and she realized it was a crab, the exact gray-green of everything around it. After that, the pool seemed to fill as she watched: a small fish darting from under a ledge, a snail dragging its shell along the bottom, the green petals of an anemone slowly opening like a hand unclenching. None of it had arrived. All of it had been there the whole time.

"Most people walk right past this pool," Teresa said on the way back, while the tourists photographed the view. "They look for something big, see nothing, and keep going."

Mara did not answer. She was annoyed to find that she wanted to go back.

By the end of the month, Teresa let her lead a walk on her own, for a group of day campers who arrived shouting and swinging their buckets. Mara took them to the bathtub pool. She crouched at its edge the way she had seen her aunt do it a dozen times, and she waited until the last of them had stopped talking. "Now," she said.

passages.title: Righter
passages.text:
The recipe box had sat on top of their grandmother's refrigerator for as long as either sister could remember: a dented tin box, painted with faded strawberries, its lid held shut by a rubber band. After the funeral, it was the only thing Lena and Ruth both asked for. Their mother, tired of mediating, told them to sort it out between themselves.

So on a Sunday in March they sat across from each other at Lena's kitchen table, the box between them. Lena, the older by six years, had already proposed a system. They would photograph every card, divide the originals by category, and each keep a complete set of copies. Ruth, who had driven three hours to get there, said that sounded fine, in the voice she used when nothing sounded fine.

The cards themselves were not what either of them had expected. Their grandmother had been a famously confident cook, but the margins of nearly every card were crowded with notes in her slanting hand. "Too salty—half next time." "Tried with honey. No." "Better with the old oven." On the card for the apple cake that had appeared at every family birthday, there were eleven dated entries, the earliest from 1962 and the last from two years ago, each changing something small.

"She never got it right," Ruth said, sounding almost delighted.

"She got it right every time," Lena said. "She just kept trying to get it righter." She heard herself and laughed, and after a moment Ruth laughed too, the first time they had laughed together since the hospital.

They abandoned Lena's system before lunch. Instead, they read the cards aloud to each other, arguing over which notes were jokes and which were serious, and by evening they had decided that neither of them would take the box. It would go back and forth between their two houses, a season at a time, and whoever had it would bake one recipe from it and add a note of her own in the margin.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: The Dust Bowl was caused mainly by a drought that no farming method could have prevented.
choices.B: Hugh Hammond Bennett was the first scientist to study how prairie grasses grow.
choices.C: The Dust Bowl crisis led the federal government to adopt new efforts to protect soil.
choices.D: Planting shelterbelts was the most effective way to end the dust storms on the Plains.

candidates.evidence: the crisis permanently changed how the federal government viewed soil
candidates.explanation: The passage moves from the storms and their causes to the federal conservation programs they prompted, and ends with the lasting change in how the government viewed soil.

A.rationale: The passage says plowing up grass made the land vulnerable, so the drought was not the only cause.

B.rationale: The passage describes Bennett's warnings about erosion, not research on how grasses grow.

D.rationale: The passage does not rank the methods and says historians still debate what ended the crisis.

hints: What does most of the passage describe happening after the storms?

strategy.explanation: Look at what the passage covers from start to finish, not one paragraph.

candidates.remember: A main idea must cover the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the phrase "dust bowl" first appeared in:

choices.A: a news report written the day after Black Sunday.
choices.B: a government report on soil erosion published in 1928.
choices.C: the text of the Soil Conservation Act signed in 1935.
choices.D: a speech that Bennett gave to farmers at a demonstration.

candidates.evidence: in a news report filed the next day, a reporter used a phrase
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says a reporter used the phrase "dust bowl" in a news report filed the day after Black Sunday.

B.rationale: The 1928 report called erosion "a national menace"; it did not use the phrase.

C.rationale: The passage does not connect the phrase to the act.

D.rationale: No such speech is mentioned.

hints: Where does paragraph 1 say the phrase was used?

strategy.explanation: Locate the phrase in paragraph 1.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: The passage indicates that the land on the southern Plains had become vulnerable to blowing mainly because:

choices.A: the wheat grown in the 1920s had roots that were too deep for the dry soil.
choices.B: farmers had plowed up the native grasses that once held the soil in place.
choices.C: the early 1930s brought unusually strong winds from the Canadian border.
choices.D: shelterbelts planted in the 1910s had been cut down to make room for farms.

candidates.evidence: Those grasses, with roots that reached deep into the ground, had held the soil in place
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the land was made vulnerable because farmers had plowed up native grasses whose deep roots had held the soil.

A.rationale: The passage says the native grasses, not the wheat, had deep roots.

C.rationale: The passage mentions drought, not unusual winds, as the natural cause.

D.rationale: The shelterbelts were planted after 1935, not in the 1910s.

hints: What had held the soil in place before the boom?

strategy.explanation: Read paragraph 2 for the long-term cause.

candidates.remember: Distinguish a long-term cause from the event that set it off.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Bennett's role in the Soil Conservation Service was to serve as its:

choices.A: chief scientific adviser.
choices.B: first regional director.
choices.C: founding legal counsel.
choices.D: first chief.

candidates.evidence: with Bennett as its first chief
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the act established the Soil Conservation Service with Bennett as its first chief.

A.rationale: The passage says he was the agency's first chief.

B.rationale: No regional role is mentioned.

C.rationale: No legal role is mentioned.

hints: What position does paragraph 3 give Bennett?

strategy.explanation: Locate the detail in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, Bennett most likely set up demonstration projects because he believed farmers would be more willing to:

choices.A: follow advice that came directly from Congress and the president.
choices.B: change their methods after reading pamphlets on soil science.
choices.C: adopt new methods after seeing them work on nearby land.
choices.D: give their damaged fields to the government to manage.

candidates.evidence: so that neighbors could see the results for themselves
candidates.explanation: Bennett doubted that lectures and pamphlets would work, so he had volunteers try methods on their own fields where neighbors could see the results.

A.rationale: He relied on farmers seeing results, not on official authority.

B.rationale: He believed pamphlets would not change how people farmed.

D.rationale: The projects worked with farmers on their own fields.

hints: What did Bennett think would not change farmers' behavior?

strategy.explanation: Contrast what Bennett rejected with what he chose.

candidates.remember: Infer a person's reasoning from what he rejects and what he chooses.

candidates.stem: The passage mentions all of the following as methods that farmers were encouraged to use EXCEPT:

choices.A: pumping groundwater to irrigate dry fields.
choices.B: plowing along the natural contours of the land.
choices.C: growing cover crops to protect bare soil.
choices.D: returning the most damaged fields to grass.

candidates.evidence: to plow along the natural contours of the land rather than in straight lines
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists contour plowing, strip cropping, cover crops, and returning fields to grass; it never mentions irrigation.

B.rationale: Paragraph 4 lists contour plowing.

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 lists cover crops.

D.rationale: Paragraph 4 lists returning damaged fields to grass.

hints: Which methods does paragraph 4 list?

strategy.explanation: Cross off each method the passage names.

candidates.remember: For EXCEPT questions, eliminate choices the passage supports.

candidates.stem: Which of the following events described in the passage happened first?

choices.A: Congress established the Soil Conservation Service.
choices.B: Bennett helped write a report calling soil erosion a national menace.
choices.C: The federal government proposed a model law for local soil conservation districts.
choices.D: A dust storm on Black Sunday darkened the afternoon across the southern Plains.

candidates.evidence: As early as 1928, he had co-authored a government report
candidates.explanation: The report came in 1928, before Black Sunday and the act (1935) and the model law (1937).

A.rationale: This happened in 1935, after the 1928 report.

C.rationale: This happened in 1937.

D.rationale: This happened in 1935.

hints: Which date in the passage is earliest?

strategy.explanation: Attach a date to each choice.

candidates.remember: Sequence questions depend on dates, not on the order of paragraphs.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "broad" most nearly means:

choices.A: physically large.
choices.B: plainly obvious.
choices.C: loosely tolerant.
choices.D: wide-ranging.

candidates.evidence: gave the agency broad authority to fight erosion on private as well as public land
candidates.explanation: The agency's authority covered both private and public land, so "broad" means wide-ranging.

A.rationale: The word describes authority, not physical size.

B.rationale: Nothing about the authority is described as obvious.

C.rationale: The point is the scope of the authority, not tolerance.

hints: What does the rest of the sentence say the authority covered?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.

candidates.stem: The last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: prove that the shelterbelts did more to stop the storms than the farming methods did.
choices.B: argue that the rain, not human effort, was solely responsible for ending the Dust Bowl.
choices.C: qualify the success of the new methods while identifying a lasting result of the crisis.
choices.D: introduce a new problem that the Soil Conservation Service would face in the 1940s.

candidates.evidence: Historians still debate how much credit belongs to the new farming methods
candidates.explanation: The paragraph notes that the rain's return makes the methods' share of credit uncertain, then states the clear lasting change in how the government viewed soil.

A.rationale: The paragraph says historians still debate the causes, so it proves nothing about which effort worked best.

B.rationale: It says credit is debated; it does not give the rain sole credit.

D.rationale: No new problem is introduced.

hints: Does the paragraph give full credit to anyone?

strategy.explanation: Identify both moves the paragraph makes.

candidates.remember: A paragraph that weighs credit and then states a firm conclusion is qualifying, not proving.

author_checklist.hardness: requires recognizing a hedge plus a firm conclusion

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that the Gee's Bend quilts are more valuable than the paintings they are compared to.
choices.B: trace how the quilts became recognized as art and question one common way of praising them.
choices.C: explain the step-by-step techniques that Gee's Bend quilters use to assemble a quilt.
choices.D: describe the political struggle over the Gee's Bend ferry between the 1960s and 2006.

candidates.evidence: To praise the quilts for resembling museum paintings
candidates.explanation: The passage follows the quilts from household necessity to museum exhibitions and ends by questioning comparisons to modern painting.

A.rationale: The author questions the comparison but does not rank the quilts above paintings.

C.rationale: The passage describes the quilts' look and history, not step-by-step technique.

D.rationale: The ferry is one detail, not the focus of the passage.

hints: What does the last paragraph add to the history in the earlier ones?

strategy.explanation: Account for both the history and the final paragraph.

candidates.remember: A purpose answer must fit every part of the passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the materials used in the quilts included:

choices.A: fabric bought from department stores in New York.
choices.B: cotton grown and woven on the former plantation.
choices.C: blankets that had been donated by the cooperative.
choices.D: work clothes, denim, feed sacks, and sewing scraps.

candidates.evidence: worn-out work clothes, faded denim, feed sacks, and scraps left over from sewing
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists worn-out work clothes, faded denim, feed sacks, and sewing scraps.

A.rationale: The stores bought quilts; the passage does not say quilters bought fabric there.

B.rationale: The passage mentions the plantation only as history.

C.rationale: No donated blankets are mentioned.

hints: What does paragraph 2 say the quilters worked with?

strategy.explanation: Locate the list in paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, one reason the Gee's Bend quilts varied so much in design was that:

choices.A: the materials the quilters had on hand varied widely.
choices.B: each quilter was trained by a different professional artist.
choices.C: department stores asked for a new pattern with every order.
choices.D: the quilters were copying modern paintings they had seen.

candidates.evidence: Because the material varied so much, the quilts did too
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the quilts varied because the material varied; quilters were also expected to work out their own designs.

B.rationale: Quilters learned from mothers and grandmothers, not professional artists.

C.rationale: Stores wanted neat, regular patterns, not constant variety.

D.rationale: The author says few quilters had seen modern painting.

hints: What does paragraph 2 say caused the variety?

strategy.explanation: Look for "Because" in paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Cause-effect answers often follow signal words like "because."

candidates.stem: According to the passage, after the ferry service ended in 1962, residents traveling to the county seat faced:

choices.A: a long walk along the riverbank.
choices.B: a toll bridge that few could afford.
choices.C: a trip of more than an hour by road.
choices.D: a boat that ran only on weekends.

candidates.evidence: leaving a trip of more than an hour by road
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the end of the ferry left residents with a trip of more than an hour by road.

A.rationale: The passage describes a road trip, not a walk.

B.rationale: No bridge is mentioned.

D.rationale: The service ended; no weekend boat is mentioned.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say replaced the ferry trip?

strategy.explanation: Locate the detail in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: Paragraph 4 most strongly suggests that the department store orders:

choices.A: were the main reason the quilts later appeared in museums.
choices.B: encouraged some quilters to move away from their usual style.
choices.C: paid too little for the quilters to continue making them.
choices.D: introduced the quilters to the paintings of abstract artists.

candidates.evidence: some quilters set their own improvised designs aside to meet them
candidates.explanation: Buyers wanted neat, regular patterns, and some quilters set their improvised designs aside, so the orders pulled them away from their usual style.

A.rationale: The museum exhibition came decades later and is not linked to the orders.

C.rationale: The passage says the orders paid well.

D.rationale: Nothing connects the orders to painting.

hints: What did buyers want, and how did some quilters respond?

strategy.explanation: Connect the buyers' wishes to the quilters' choices.

candidates.remember: Inferences must follow directly from what the text states.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the 2002 exhibition first opened at:

choices.A: the Whitney Museum of American Art.
choices.B: a gallery at the county courthouse.
choices.C: a department store in New York City.
choices.D: the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

candidates.evidence: opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, and then traveled to the Whitney
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 says the exhibition opened in Houston and then traveled to the Whitney.

A.rationale: The exhibition traveled to the Whitney after opening in Houston.

B.rationale: No such gallery is mentioned.

C.rationale: Stores bought quilts in the 1960s; the exhibition was in museums.

hints: Where did the exhibition open, and where did it go next?

strategy.explanation: Note the order of the two museums.

candidates.remember: Watch for answers that name the right place at the wrong time.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "improvised" most nearly means:

choices.A: composed without a fixed plan.
choices.B: repaired after being damaged.
choices.C: produced with poor materials.
choices.D: performed in front of others.

candidates.evidence: set their own improvised designs aside
candidates.explanation: The improvised designs contrast with neat, regular patterns, so they were composed freely rather than from a fixed plan.

B.rationale: Nothing about repair is described.

C.rationale: The word describes how designs were made, not material quality.

D.rationale: No performance is involved.

hints: What kind of pattern did the buyers want instead?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use the contrast in the sentence to define the word.

candidates.stem: The author's attitude toward comparing the quilts to abstract paintings can best be described as:

choices.A: enthusiastic, because the comparisons prove the quilts are art.
choices.B: dismissive, because the comparisons brought the quilters no benefit.
choices.C: concerned that the comparisons misrepresent the quilters' tradition.
choices.D: uncertain, because it is unclear whether the quilters saw such art.

candidates.evidence: they can also be misleading
candidates.explanation: The author grants the comparisons' benefits but argues they can mislead by implying the quilts needed a painter's approval.

A.rationale: The author says the comparisons can be misleading.

B.rationale: The author grants that they brought attention and income.

D.rationale: The author states plainly that few quilters had seen modern painting.

hints: What does the author grant, and what does the author object to?

strategy.explanation: Read the whole last paragraph, including the concession.

candidates.remember: An author can grant a benefit and still object.

author_checklist.hardness: must weigh a concession against the main objection

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, the irregular features of many Gee's Bend quilts, such as wandering borders and broken patterns, most likely reflect:

choices.A: a lack of training among the women who made them.
choices.B: deliberate choices made within the community's own tradition.
choices.C: the influence of the abstract paintings shown in Houston and New York.
choices.D: instructions given to them by the department store buyers.

candidates.evidence: were expected to work out designs of their own
candidates.explanation: Quilters were taught by family and expected to create their own designs, and the author calls their tradition one of individual choice.

A.rationale: Quilters learned from family and were expected to create their own designs.

C.rationale: The quilts long predate the 2002 exhibition.

D.rationale: Buyers wanted regular patterns, not irregular ones.

hints: What were quilters expected to do with their designs?

strategy.explanation: Combine paragraph 2 with the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: Choose the inference the text supports, not one it contradicts.

candidates.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: how one clockmaker solved the problem of finding longitude at sea.
choices.B: why astronomy proved to be the best way to find a ship's position.
choices.C: how the British Parliament organized its navy in the eighteenth century.
choices.D: the dangers that sailors faced from storms and disease at sea.

candidates.evidence: his breakthrough was a fourth timekeeper
candidates.explanation: The passage explains the longitude problem and then focuses on Harrison's decades of work on the clocks that solved it.

B.rationale: The passage ends with Harrison's chronometers becoming standard, not astronomy.

C.rationale: The passage mentions Parliament only in connection with the longitude prize.

D.rationale: Dangers are mentioned only as consequences of wrong longitude.

hints: Who is the central figure for most of the passage?

strategy.explanation: Consider what most paragraphs are about.

candidates.remember: A main idea must cover the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, sailors could determine latitude by:

choices.A: comparing the local time with the time at their ship's home port.
choices.B: observing the moon's position against the stars.
choices.C: measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon.
choices.D: timing how long it took to sail between two islands with known positions.

candidates.evidence: by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says latitude could be found by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon.

A.rationale: This is how longitude, not latitude, is calculated.

B.rationale: This was the proposed astronomical method for longitude.

D.rationale: No such method is mentioned.

hints: Which position does paragraph 1 call easy to find, and how?

strategy.explanation: Keep latitude and longitude separate.

candidates.remember: Watch for details that belong to a different part of the topic.

candidates.stem: Based on the information in paragraph 1, a navigator whose local time was two hours earlier than home-port time could conclude that the ship had traveled:

choices.A: 30 degrees east of the home port.
choices.B: 30 degrees west of the home port.
choices.C: 15 degrees west of the home port.
choices.D: 2 degrees west of the home port.

candidates.evidence: Because Earth turns 15 degrees every hour
candidates.explanation: At 15 degrees per hour, a two-hour difference equals 30 degrees; local time behind home-port time means the sun reaches the ship later, so the ship is west of home.

A.rationale: Local time behind home-port time means the ship is west of home, not east.

C.rationale: Two hours at 15 degrees per hour is 30 degrees, not 15.

D.rationale: This confuses hours with degrees.

hints: How many degrees does Earth turn in one hour?

strategy.explanation: Multiply the time difference by 15.

candidates.remember: Apply a rule stated in the passage to a new case.

author_checklist.hardness: applies the stated rate plus direction reasoning

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the Longitude Act offered a prize for a method that could determine longitude to within:

choices.A: one full degree.
choices.B: fifteen degrees.
choices.C: five seconds.
choices.D: half a degree.

candidates.evidence: to within half a degree
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the prize was for a method accurate to within half a degree.

A.rationale: The act required accuracy to within half a degree.

B.rationale: Fifteen degrees is how far Earth turns in an hour.

C.rationale: Five seconds is how much the fourth timekeeper lost.

hints: What standard does paragraph 2 give?

strategy.explanation: Match the number to the right detail.

candidates.remember: Watch for numbers taken from other parts of the passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, pendulum clocks were poorly suited for use at sea because:

choices.A: a ship's motion disrupted their swinging pendulums.
choices.B: their wooden parts absorbed moisture from the damp air.
choices.C: they could not be set to the time at the home port.
choices.D: their oily woods made the moving parts too slippery.

candidates.evidence: swinging pendulums, which a ship's motion threw into disorder
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a ship's motion threw pendulums into disorder.

B.rationale: The passage blames motion and metal parts, not wood.

C.rationale: Setting the time is not described as the difficulty.

D.rationale: Oily woods were Harrison's solution, not a problem.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say happened to pendulums at sea?

strategy.explanation: Locate the cause in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Answer cause-effect questions from the stated cause.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that Harrison chose naturally oily woods for his early clocks mainly to:

choices.A: make the clocks light enough to carry on small ships.
choices.B: avoid relying on lubricants that broke down over time.
choices.C: protect the clocks from changes in temperature.
choices.D: show that a carpenter could build better clocks than scientists.

candidates.evidence: so that the moving parts needed no lubricant
candidates.explanation: The oily woods meant the parts needed no lubricant, which in other clocks thickened and failed.

A.rationale: Weight is not given as the reason.

C.rationale: Temperature effects are discussed with metal parts, not with oily woods.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests this motive.

hints: What problem with other clocks does paragraph 4 mention?

strategy.explanation: Read the full sentence about the woods.

candidates.remember: Look for the reason stated with "so that."

candidates.stem: According to the passage, after his first sea clock performed well, Harrison:

choices.A: immediately claimed the prize offered by Parliament.
choices.B: tested it on a voyage to Jamaica.
choices.C: gave its design to the Board of Longitude.
choices.D: asked for support to build an improved clock.

candidates.evidence: Harrison asked for support to build a better one
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that rather than claim a reward, Harrison asked for support to build a better clock.

A.rationale: He asked for support rather than claiming a reward.

B.rationale: The Jamaica voyage tested his fourth timekeeper.

C.rationale: The board demanded his designs much later.

hints: What did Harrison do instead of claiming a reward?

strategy.explanation: Track which clock each event involves.

candidates.remember: Keep events matched to the right stage of the story.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "favor" most nearly means:

choices.A: assist.
choices.B: resemble.
choices.C: prefer.
choices.D: reward.

candidates.evidence: continued to favor the astronomical method
candidates.explanation: The board kept preferring astronomy over Harrison's clocks.

A.rationale: The board was not helping the astronomical method; it preferred it.

B.rationale: Nothing about resemblance is described.

D.rationale: The board withheld rewards; "favor" describes its preference.

hints: Which method did the board keep choosing?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.

candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that Harrison's approach succeeded despite the board's resistance.
choices.B: suggest that Harrison's clocks were soon replaced by a better astronomical method.
choices.C: explain why the Board of Longitude never awarded the official prize.
choices.D: reveal that Harrison earned a fortune from the sale of chronometers.

candidates.evidence: copies of his design, known as marine chronometers, were becoming standard equipment
candidates.explanation: After describing the board's reluctance, the passage ends by noting that chronometers based on his design became standard, confirming his approach.

B.rationale: The sentence says copies of his design became standard.

C.rationale: The reasons are given earlier; the last sentence describes later adoption.

D.rationale: The sentence says nothing about Harrison's earnings.

hints: What does "however" contrast the last sentence with?

strategy.explanation: Read the last sentence against the paragraph before it.

candidates.remember: A contrast word at the end of a passage often signals the author's final point.

author_checklist.hardness: function judged against the preceding contrast

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.A: A girl competes with her aunt to find the rarest animals in a tide pool.
choices.B: A reluctant visitor learns the value of patient watching and later passes it on.
choices.C: A group of tourists persuades a guide to change how she leads her walks.
choices.D: A girl searches all month for a better phone signal and finally finds one by the sea.

candidates.evidence: She crouched at its edge the way she had seen her aunt do it
candidates.explanation: Mara begins impatient and uninterested, discovers what waiting reveals, and ends by leading campers the same way.

A.rationale: There is no competition; Mara learns from her aunt.

C.rationale: The tourists do not change Teresa's method.

D.rationale: The phone detail opens the story, but the story is about the tide pool.

hints: How has Mara changed by the last paragraph?

strategy.explanation: Compare Mara at the beginning and at the end.

candidates.remember: A narrative's main idea usually involves a change.

candidates.stem: The first paragraph mainly suggests that, at the start of her visit, Mara was:

choices.A: eager to learn about the animals that lived along the coast.
choices.B: worried that her aunt would be angry if she did not help.
choices.C: uninterested in the activities her aunt's home had to offer.
choices.D: excited to meet the tourists who would join the walks.

candidates.evidence: when Mara ran out of excuses, she went along
candidates.explanation: Mara cared mostly about internet access and avoided the walks until she ran out of excuses.

A.rationale: She agreed to come only on condition of internet access.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests fear of her aunt's anger.

D.rationale: She went only after she ran out of excuses.

hints: Why did Mara finally go on a walk?

strategy.explanation: Look at Mara's conditions and excuses.

candidates.remember: Infer a character's attitude from her choices.

candidates.stem: When Teresa says they are waiting "for the pool to forget we're here" (paragraph 3), she most likely means that:

choices.A: the animals will come out of hiding once the people stay still long enough.
choices.B: the water will become clearer after the waves stop disturbing it.
choices.C: the tourists will soon become bored and leave the pool to her alone.
choices.D: the tide will soon rise and fill the pool with new animals from the open sea.

candidates.evidence: None of it had arrived. All of it had been there the whole time.
candidates.explanation: The animals were present all along and appeared once the watchers were still, so Teresa means the creatures will reveal themselves when the people stop disturbing them.

B.rationale: Teresa refers to the people's presence, not to waves.

C.rationale: She wants the tourists to stay and watch.

D.rationale: The animals "had been there the whole time"; nothing new arrives.

hints: Where did the animals Mara sees come from?

strategy.explanation: Use what happens next to interpret the statement.

candidates.remember: Interpret figurative language using later events.

author_checklist.hardness: figurative statement interpreted against a later revelation

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the first animal Mara notices is a:

choices.A: fish.
choices.B: snail.
choices.C: gull.
choices.D: crab.

candidates.evidence: Then a rock she had been staring at for two full minutes moved, and she realized it was a crab
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the first thing Mara notices is a rock that turns out to be a crab.

A.rationale: The fish appears after Mara notices the crab.

B.rationale: The snail appears after the crab.

C.rationale: The gull is overhead and is not in the pool.

hints: What does Mara see first after the long wait?

strategy.explanation: Follow the order in paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: Watch for details that occur later in the sequence.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "tolerate" most nearly means:

choices.A: forgive.
choices.B: endure.
choices.C: allow.
choices.D: survive.

candidates.evidence: It took longer than Mara thought anyone would tolerate
candidates.explanation: Mara thinks the wait is longer than anyone would put up with.

A.rationale: No one is being forgiven.

C.rationale: The point is enduring the wait, not granting permission.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests danger to anyone's life.

hints: What is hard to tolerate in this sentence?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.

candidates.stem: The statement that Mara "was annoyed to find that she wanted to go back" (paragraph 6) suggests that Mara:

choices.A: was angry that her aunt had made her leave the pool so soon.
choices.B: wanted to return to her home before the end of July.
choices.C: had begun to enjoy the walks despite her earlier attitude.
choices.D: disliked the tourists and hoped to avoid them in the future.

candidates.evidence: She was annoyed to find that she wanted to go back.
candidates.explanation: Mara is annoyed because her new interest contradicts the indifference she started with.

A.rationale: Her annoyance is directed at her own feelings, not at her aunt.

B.rationale: "Go back" refers to the pool, not her home.

D.rationale: Nothing in her reaction concerns the tourists.

hints: Why might wanting to go back annoy someone who agreed to come only for the internet?

strategy.explanation: Connect paragraph 6 to paragraph 1.

candidates.remember: A character can be annoyed by her own change of heart.

candidates.stem: In the last paragraph, Mara's waiting "until the last of them had stopped talking" before saying "Now" mainly serves to show that she:

choices.A: has adopted her aunt's method of patient observation.
choices.B: is too shy to speak in front of a group of children.
choices.C: dislikes the noisy day campers she has been asked to guide.
choices.D: plans to lead the walk differently than her aunt did.

candidates.evidence: "Now," she said.
candidates.explanation: Mara repeats her aunt's crouch, her wait, and her word "Now," showing she has taken on Teresa's method.

B.rationale: She leads the walk and speaks when she chooses.

C.rationale: Waiting for quiet is part of the method, not a sign of dislike.

D.rationale: She does it "the way she had seen her aunt do it."

hints: Where else in the passage does someone say "Now"?

strategy.explanation: Compare the ending with paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Repeated words and actions often signal a character's change.

author_checklist.hardness: echo of an earlier scene must be recognized

candidates.stem: Which of the following events occurs last in the passage?

choices.A: Teresa explains that most people walk past the pool.
choices.B: Mara notices a snail moving along the bottom of the pool.
choices.C: A child asks what the group is waiting for.
choices.D: Mara leads a group of day campers to the pool.

candidates.evidence: By the end of the month, Teresa let her lead a walk on her own
candidates.explanation: Mara leads the campers at the end of the month, after all the other events.

A.rationale: This happens on the way back from the first walk.

B.rationale: This happens during the first walk.

C.rationale: This happens during the first walk.

hints: What happens "by the end of the month"?

strategy.explanation: Use time markers to order events.

candidates.remember: Sequence questions depend on time markers.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the card for the apple cake contained:

choices.A: eleven dated entries, the earliest of them from 1962.
choices.B: a single note saying the recipe should never be changed.
choices.C: instructions written by the sisters' mother.
choices.D: a list of the birthdays when the cake had been served.

candidates.evidence: there were eleven dated entries, the earliest from 1962
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the card had eleven dated entries, the earliest from 1962, each changing something small.

B.rationale: The card has many entries, each changing something.

C.rationale: The notes are in the grandmother's hand.

D.rationale: The entries record changes, not birthdays.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say about the apple cake card?

strategy.explanation: Locate the detail in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

revision_history.reason: both blind solvers: "spanning roughly six decades" assumed a present-day date the passage never gives
revision_history.change: key now cites only the stated earliest date
